summary: This Best Current Practice describes how IANA can hand out protocol code points early, before a specification is finished, when implementers need real values to test with. It addresses the problem that the usual Standards Action rule only assigns values after publication. It was replaced by RFC 7120.

eli5.summary: Imagine reserving a seat number for a show before the tickets are officially printed, so rehearsals can start. This note explains when that early reservation is allowed.

subtitle: When IANA hands out protocol code points before a standard is final

tldr.problem: Protocol standards need to allocate code points, but the 'Standards Action' rule only assigns them after publication. Early implementations need real values to test interoperability before the RFC is finished, creating a deadlock.
tldr.mechanism: IANA can make early allocations of code points from 'Standards Action' spaces, marking them as temporary and valid for one year. Conditions: the code space must allow it, the spec must be stable and Standards Track, and the community must want early implementation.
tldr.outcome: This breaks the deadlock. If the RFC is published, the allocation becomes permanent. If the draft fails, the allocations are deprecated and eventually recycled.

facts.label: Maximum renewals
facts.value: 1, plus rare exceptions reviewed by IESG

today: RFC 4020 is an Internet Best Current Practice. It was later updated by RFC 7120, which gives more detail on early allocation for routing-area code points. It is not obsolete but often cited alongside its successor.

sections.title: The Early Allocation Problem
sections.content:
Standards Track RFCs often define code points—like message types, error codes, or protocol identifiers—that implementers need to know before publication. The normal IANA rule for such allocations is Standards Action, which requires a published RFC to finalize the values.

This creates a catch-22: to test a draft RFC, you need the final code point values, but you can only get them after the RFC is published. Early implementations have worked around this by guessing unused values, but if IANA later assigns different values, implementations won't interoperate.

This BCP formalizes early allocation: a way for IANA to hand out code points before publication, under strict conditions.
sections.eli5: When a game is still being designed, the rules might say 'three-letter words are worth 10 points', but we don't know which three-letter words yet. With early allocation, we can reserve some values now, test them, and keep them if the game ships.

sections.title: When Early Allocation Is Allowed
sections.content:
Early allocation is only allowed when four conditions hold:

(a) The code point space must be marked 'Standards Action' by IESG and must have been approved for early allocation. (b) The draft must be Standards Track and the specs must be adequately described—implementers must know what the code points do. (c) The specifications must be stable: changes must not break earlier implementations. (d) There must be real community interest in early implementation and deployment.

If (a) or (b) are not met, early allocation does not happen. The WG chairs and Area Director assess whether (c) and (d) are true.
sections.eli5: Four things must be true: the game's authority has to allow it, the rules have to be written down clearly, the rules can't change after people start playing, and people have to actually want to play early.

sections.title: The Early Allocation Process
sections.content:
The authors request early allocation from the WG chairs, naming the code points they need. The WG chairs check the conditions, gauge community consensus, and (with Area Director approval) ask IANA for the allocation.

IANA marks the codes as temporary and valid for one year from the allocation date. The date is made public. Internet Drafts should not name specific values until this allocation happens.

When the RFC progresses to publication, the authors remind IANA to remove the 'temporary' tag and make the allocation permanent. If the draft fails or expires, the WG chairs tell IANA to mark the codes as deprecated, and eventually they may be recycled for reuse.
sections.eli5: Step 1: Ask for numbers. Step 2: IANA gives them but marks them 'one year only'. Step 3: If the game ships, the numbers become permanent. If not, they go back.

sections.title: Risks and Safeguards
sections.content:
The main risks are code point space depletion (many early allocations, few succeed to publication) and overloading IANA's process. This memo addresses both: early allocations require IESG and WG approval, preventing casual requests, and IANA is not responsible for tracking status or expiry—the WG chairs are. The one-year limit and one-renewal rule also bound the risk.

The processes here are designed to have minimal impact on IANA itself.
sections.eli5: Danger: too many temporary bookings and IANA gets swamped, or the game authors forget to clean up. The memo sets limits: limited renewals, the authors do the paperwork, IANA just marks and unmarks.

references.text: Narten, T. and H. Alvestrand, "Guidelines for Writing an IANA Considerations Section in RFCs", BCP 26, RFC 2434, October 1998.
